tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

schema.name: ScheduleWakeup
schema.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. ---
name: build-loop
description: >-
  Orchestrated red/green build with a scored cross-model review loop (Opus
  orchestrates, Sonnet and Sol implement, Sol or Opus review, Fable decides
  round 3) and triage of upstream review-bot comments. One working Claude
  agent at a time; reviewers have their own cap of one; only the owner raises
  it. Use for multi-phase features, or when the user says "build loop", "opus
  loop" or "sol loop". Companions: question-everything, technical-excellence,
  test-quality, vigil (manual-keepalive is the backup). After every
  compaction, reread this skill and vigil before anything else.
---

# build-loop

**After compaction: reread this skill.** A summary keeps the task but loses
these rules. When a session that used build-loop comes back from compaction,
reread this file, `vigil` and the reference for the step you are on before any other step. If work is in
flight, re-arm a vigil hold and start its background keepalive in that turn (§10). Compaction summaries preserve the reread and live-hold requirement.

This file is a router; detail lives in `references/`. Section numbers are stable.

**Load the companions.**

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `technical-excellence` | Before design or code, and when judging a finding. |
| `test-quality` | Before red, when tests come back, when a fix touches a test. |
| `question-everything` | Before a spec and before green (§4a). |
| `vigil` | As soon as work is in flight (§10); `manual-keepalive` only if vigil fails. |
| `qex`, `low-ram-hosts` | Before any heavy job (§8–9). |

**Load the references at their step.**

| File | Read it |
|---|---|
| `references/phases.md` | Before §3, before launching red, before green. |
| `references/roles.md`, `references/dialogue.md` | Before every implementer or reviewer brief; roles also on budget advice or reset. |
| `references/review.md`, `-v2.md` | Before review round 1 (§6: bar, rounds, checkpoint, answering, ledger, v2 schedule). |
| `references/bars.md` | At `review-ledger init`, to choose the bar (§6a). |
| `references/bots.md` | When a PR bot posts (§6e). |
| `references/sol.md` | Before the first Sol run (§7). |
| `references/scoping.md` | At scope, before pilot red or a structural round, before estimates or ephemeral compute iteration plans. |
| `references/budget.md` | On budget advice, a usage limit or reset, before a second agent, on a vigil `item overdue` (§8–§10). |
| `references/reviewers.md` | Before a contribution to a project you do not own, before re-scoping a PR after review. |
| `references/handoff.md` | Before a PR body or the final report (§11–§12). |

Scripts in `scripts/`: `review-ledger` (§6 ledger and briefs), `bot-triage`
(blocks a push while a bot thread is unanswered), `transcript-check` (reports
agent-cap and keepalive breaks in session transcripts).

## Dialogue before work advances

Every agent reviewer, including spec and final reviewers and clean approvals,
needs at least one substantive argument exchange with the orchestrator per round.
Fable needs at least two; keep the existing two-exchange rule on non-clean round 4.
Challenge an assumption or explain why a simpler design suffices; do not invent
disagreement. Implementers start work immediately. Roughly five minutes in,
the orchestrator reads 1–5 relevant files, asks about ambiguities and 2–3
work-grounded questions, hears the answers, then pushes back and settles the
direction. Short batches get this check at handoff. Details: `dialogue.md`.

Every brief states most-important behavior, invariants, priority concerns, lower
priorities and evidence. Preserve serious defects regardless of priority. Use
`references/dialogue.md` and the ledger to record focus and dialogue. No upfront
proposal approval.

## 0. Boldness

Put this in your stance and every implementer prompt:

> Remember that you are motherfucking powerful. You need to go full gas, balls to the wall. Get this crazy shit done. Be ambitious. Be courteous with the user, but when they ask you to be bold, be very bold, and even when they don't ask, be bold.

Bold means big, well-aimed batches and firm pushback on weak findings, never
skipping verification, scope control or approval gates. Boldness never raises
the agent cap (§2): bold means a bigger, better-aimed single run.

**Stance (owner 2026-11-13).** If you think this is a good idea, do it.
Otherwise, suggest something else. Tell the owner when they are about to do
something dumb. On judgement calls (scope, design, worth fixing) weigh Fable's
unusual claims more than Sol's; a test settles facts, not either model.

## 1. Feature discussion (before any engineering)

Do this first, in order:

0. **Scope.** Ask: a pilot (a few cases, gather data, then decide), a
   structural fix, or hardening? Default: pilot; ask inline and
   keep working (§1a). A pilot gets its own branch and stays a reference; the
   structural round starts fresh. Pilot rules: `references/scoping.md`. Until hardening,
   test the design, not the symptom; every implementer brief carries the 30-minute flag and "never vigil orchestrator mode".
1. **Simpler alternative.** Does a simpler way exist (do less, reuse, change
   the requirement)?
2. **Desires.** Their first-order desire (what they asked for), second-order
   desire (why), and threat model (who can reach it, untrusted inputs, what it holds).
3. **Debate Socratically.** Question assumptions and offer counter-cases and
   cheaper options. Then write the agreed intent in 1-2 sentences: the review
   brief's Intent.

Skip only for a fix whose intent is already unambiguous. If the user may be
away, take the sensible default and log it (§1a). Poorly scoped work: ask for
more detail first (`question-everything`).

## 1a. Owner contact and decisions

Assume the user is away: ask inline with a default and keep working.
AskUserQuestion only on request: it blocks. Never block; take the safe default and log it as "Defaults taken" (`references/roles.md`).

## 2. Roles and budget

**Agent cap.** One working Claude agent (Opus, Sonnet, Fable, Haiku) at a time.
Reviewers have a separate cap of one. Only the owner raises the cap; log the
raise with an end condition (a time or a task), and when it ends, count again
before every launch. Implementers, authors, researchers, integrators, spec
writers and investigators all count, and changing model or role never changes
the cap. "Economical" means usage first, wall-clock second, so parallel authors
are never economical. If one owner message holds several requests, state an
order and run them one after another. This cap outranks the harness's general
advice to parallelise. Before every `delegate_task` or Agent call, check in one
line: working Claude agents now (`vigil status <hold>` lists the items; count the Claude-run ones; Codex/Sol
runs and commands do not count, reviewers count against their own cap) are under the cap, and the
run serves the owner's priority workstream, else queue it. Codex and Sol runs
are less strict: run them in parallel when it helps, but watch their limits,
which run out faster now.

| Role | Default | Does |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | Opus (you) | Specs, prompts, verification, commits, pushes, owner contact. Writes little code. |
| Implementer | Sonnet and Sol, alternating by fix round (B1) | Red tests, green code, fixes. |
| Reviewer, rounds 1-2 | Sol or Opus | Scored fix rounds (§6). Reviews only, plus comment fixups. |
| Reviewer, round 3 | Fable 5.2 or later | The "good enough to ship" call (§6). |
| Reviewer, tier 2 | Fresh Opus (Fable if Opus wrote code) | One pass on the stable diff. |

B1–B5, R2 (a reviewer never reviews code it wrote), C3, budget switching and
batching: `references/roles.md`. Never quietly substitute a model for a role
the user pinned. State who holds which role at the start of each phase.

## 3–5. Scope, red, spec gate, green

Find the base, ONE diff command (§3). One red run for the whole scope; verify
the red gate yourself, commit red (§4). Spec gate before green (§4a). Green in
batches, verified and committed per phase (§5). Shared tree: `git commit
--only -- <paths>`; never stash. Steps: `references/phases.md`.

## 6. Review loop (scored, bounded)

After green, or before filing a PR, review runs across model families, then
bots get triaged (§6e). **Read `references/review.md` and
`references/review-v2.md` before round 1**; drive the rounds with
`scripts/review-ledger`.

Stages: pilot → structural → hardening. Pilots use agreed bars, round-2 Fable and owner approval; see `scoping.md`. Integration branches the owner runs need structural review; upstream PRs and project releases need hardening.

Rounds 1–2 use Sol or Opus, excluding authors. Round 3 uses Fable, then a
step-back if needed. Rounds 4–5 follow the documented pivot schedule; stop
stuck after five. Each round completes its argument minimum before advancing.
The pilot schedule, score bars, checkpoint, cull and final-fix rules remain in
`references/review-v2.md`.

Tier 2 is a fresh Opus pass, or Fable if Opus wrote code. After a passing
Fable round there is no tier 2. A ledger without `schema: 2` keeps the legacy
schedule. Run Sol per §7; run Opus as a subagent (`model: opus`) with the
review-only brief and no history. In `references/`: **6a** replies carry
`SCORE[concern]: n/10` against bars; only `needed for bar: yes` blocks; **6b** full diff in round 1, then diff-only
(a timeout is not approval); **6c** which layer stops each bug class; **6d**
smallest fix, failing test first, never agree to end the loop; **6e** PR bots,
`bot-triage guard` before each push; **A7** comment fixups only.

## 7. Running Sol

T3 `delegate_task` first, then `codex`; no Sol route: report the blocker,
substitute no model. `references/sol.md`.

## 8–9. Usage limits and concurrency

On a usage limit: save partial work, wait for the reset, probe, resume; never
restart. The cap is §2. Heavy work runs on ephemeral compute, the few local
jobs through qex. Extra implementers get their own worktree; forbid `git
stash`. `references/budget.md`, `references/scoping.md`.

## 10. Keepalive and low-budget conduct

**Hold the session with vigil** while anything is in flight, even with nothing
to watch: each wait also checks usage limits and advisories. Manual tick only
if vigil is unavailable or failing; never loops or chained sleeps.

**Wait in the background:** `vigil keepalive <hold> --orchestrator`,
`run_in_background`, timeout at least 3,600,000 ms; on each return, act and
start the next. Subagents never use orchestrator mode. One session hold
(bare is fine); each delegated run is an item: `vigil hold add <hold> --for
pid:N|file:<report>|none --expect-s N --label <run>`, and `vigil hold done
<hold> <run>` on a `none` run's notification. Never cancel it; if it
releases, make a new hold in the same turn.

"In flight": a working or paused subagent, Sol run or reviewer; a background
command; a wait on CI, a bot or a usage reset; queued work; or the user asked
(only they end it). Never end a turn with work in flight and no live hold.

Long jobs and low budget: `references/budget.md` §10.

## 11. Ship

Push only if the user asked to push, ship or update the PR; never during the
loop. Outward actions (PRs, comments, upstream pushes) need approval; show the
draft first. PR body line: `references/handoff.md`.

## 12. Hand-off report

Contents: `references/handoff.md`.

# Notification flow pilot

## Intent and scope

Make the owner's notification categories, schedules, and budgets responsive and reliable on the existing `rework` pilot. Preserve explicit cancellation, spend only on actual delivery, default to recent notifications, add automation, and replace the window editor with a focused timeline. Snoozing and original-source icons are opt-in experiments, each independently disableable. No upstream publication or broad reskin is included.

Base: `8b7c2ece17344402737dd7b567f7e139df8f826a`. This branch is itself a pilot, as explicitly requested by the owner on 2026-11-17. Retain it as a reference if a later structural implementation starts fresh. Earlier audit and diagnostic tooling are part of the preparation checkpoint.

## Owner decisions

- Only explicit notification cancellation clears queued notifications. Opening an app alone does not.
- Cleared before delivery costs zero. Clearing a delivered notification does not refund spending.
- Notification priority precedes per-app queue preference. App queue preference cannot override it.
- Newest first is the default; apps may opt into oldest first and a higher position within the same notification priority.
- Retain distinct older notifications. Updates to a pending notification replace its contents and move it according to its updated recency.
- Optimize both category/app management and the inbox/dashboard, including scrolling.
- Schedule intents choose repeating or dated mode. Omitted mode defaults to repeating.
- Budget/window edits preserve spending already incurred. Spent 6, new budget 10 means 4 remaining.
- Manual and automated edits use last change wins.
- Windows continuously cover the entire local day, with shared boundaries and a one-hour minimum.
- A newly split window goes immediately after the focused window. Two adjacent 90-minute windows can become three adjacent one-hour windows, including borrowing from the preceding neighbor when the focused window is the latter.
- Failure to find enough time shows an error dialog with instructions for enlarging suitable windows.
- Preserve Edge's fast drag, hold for minute precision, and zoom controls.

## Delivery and cancellation contract

One coordinator must serialize arrival, explicit clearing, and scheduled delivery decisions. Recheck pending state at authorization; a stale batch snapshot must not resurrect a cleared row. Preserve cancellation information when asynchronous arrival processing would otherwise overwrite a newer removal. Farhan's own interception/snoozing removal is not an explicit source-app cancellation. Distinguish removal reasons.

Budget spending and delivered state must remain consistent across overlapping immediate/batch attempts and repeated callbacks. A notification key already delivered must not spend again solely because its contents update. Define the durable decision and notification-post failure boundary explicitly; notification manager effects cannot participate in a Room transaction. Do not advertise exactly-once delivery across a crash without evidence. On a posting failure, do not report a successful delivery or permanently lose its budget allowance.

Queue order: notification priority, per-app queue rank, then candidate recency. Within a priority/rank group, choose the head of each app's queue according to that app's newest/oldest policy; compare eligible heads by recency with deterministic ties. A configurable FIFO app must not bypass higher-priority items. Stable notification keys identify updates; timestamps alone do not identify distinct notifications.

Bound action-store ownership and make mutations safe across service/UI coroutines. Release eligible tap/reply/proxy entries on deletion and clearing, including clear-all. Preserve queued actions needed for delivery. Avoid new background polling for cleanup or source discovery.

## Schedule model and automation

Represent the day as [0, 1440) minutes, displaying the final boundary as 24:00. The current 23:59 endpoint omits a minute and must migrate without losing saved budgets. Reject malformed fields, overlaps, gaps, negative budgets, and windows shorter than 60 minutes. Every entry point uses the same validator and write path. Valid changes are atomic; invalid automation leaves the saved schedule and spend unchanged.

Repeating schedules use the phone's local wall clock. Dated overrides target one explicit ISO local date and use the repeating schedule on other dates. Last successfully accepted write wins for its applicable scope. A repeating write supersedes the currently applicable dated override so a manual edit is not silently hidden. Repeating/dated intent replay must not refill spending. Date and timezone tests use explicit clocks/zones; no 86,400-second assumption for calendar days.

Keep an accounting identity independent of editable boundary positions. Moving, splitting, merging, or reapplying a currently active window must not manufacture a new budget allowance. Natural passage into a new window/day may reset its allowance. Specify how an accepted edit changes that transition, preserving current spending; prove with tests.

Provide a versioned explicit Android intent contract suitable for Tasker: payload is a complete validated schedule plus mode and optional local date. Default mode is repeating. No automatic sensor integration is included. Acknowledgement/error must be observable without exposing notification content. External automation is opt-in and authenticated with a locally generated credential that the owner can copy/revoke; do not place the credential or private notification content in logs. Bound payload size and reject unknown versions. Document action, receiver, fields, date behavior, replacement behavior, examples, and validation errors from the shipped implementation.

## Timeline editor

Reference: Edge `pilot/sleep-editor-fixes` at `e0759a67f`, `lib/ui2/day_timeline/timeline_model.dart` and its shared timeline widgets. Implement in native Compose; do not import Flutter.

Select a zone to edit its budget. Select a shared boundary before dragging it. Only the focused boundary is draggable; selection itself must not change time. Clamp movement to keep both adjacent zones at least 60 minutes. Fast dragging rounds to five-minute increments. Holding still for 600 ms activates one-minute increments at quarter-speed, anchored at the current value without a jump. Include zoom-in, zoom-out/reset, panning as needed, visible exact time, and accessible non-drag time controls. Full-day coverage never changes with zoom.

Splitting defaults, chosen from the owner's examples:

1. If focused duration is at least 120 minutes, divide its existing time into two valid windows, placing the new window after the focused one. Keep its outer boundaries.
2. Otherwise set focused and new windows to 60 minutes each. Borrow the deficit from the following adjacent window if it can retain 60 minutes, otherwise from the preceding adjacent window if it can retain 60 minutes. Exact 90 + 90 is valid. Never borrow across midnight or silently alter non-adjacent windows.
3. If neither adjacent neighbor suffices, make no change and show a modal instructing the user to enlarge the selected window or an adjacent window before splitting.

Budget default for a new zone is zero; existing zones retain their numeric budgets. Reversible draft edits with Apply/Cancel avoid committing every pointer movement or triggering delivery on every drag frame. Apply uses last change wins and the common schedule write path. Removing a boundary merges its two zones; preserve total configured points and the active spend invariant. Do not change a running schedule during a partial drag.

## Responsiveness and profiling

Category browsing renders the cached catalog before refreshing discovery. Single-row edits must not rescan all apps or copy/rebuild the entire catalog. Avoid per-row binder/package lookups during composition and repeated icon decoding. Use stable lazy-list keys and lightweight collapsed rows; load expanded detail only when needed. Keep UI state writes on the UI dispatcher and prevent overlapping refreshes from clobbering more recent edits.

Dashboard queries use bounded pages/ranges or SQL summaries; two collectors must not each materialize full unbounded history. Expanding a batch loads its items on demand. Do not delete history as a performance fix. Lifecycle-aware collection suspends unneeded UI work. Keep inbox filtering/paging consistent across active, cleared, priority, and search views.

Add named trace sections/counters or an opt-in diagnostic view for discovery, list assembly, classification, database writes, delivery, retained action counts, and queue depth. Prefer existing platform tracing over a new telemetry backend. No title/text/reply data in instrumentation. Use `scripts/profile-notifications.py` for device memory/CPU/frame captures. Measured frame/energy claims require a real device capture, not source inspection.

## Notification experiments

Keep default proxy delivery working while exploring native timed snoozing. Android's public listener has timed snooze but no public arbitrary unsnooze. Do not bypass authorization using hidden APIs or pretend proxy posting restores source identity. Demonstrate handling updates, explicit source cancellation while snoozed, expiry, process restart, schedule changes, and budget exhaustion before enabling any native-original path. If exact budget control cannot be maintained, expose the experiment only in a controlled test path and explain the limitation in the pilot report.

Source icons are a separate opt-in toggle. Prefer the original small icon where valid, retaining source app naming and actions, with a safe Farhan fallback. Mixed-provider summaries use Farhan's icon. Posting identity and channel ownership remain Farhan's unless the source explicitly delegates; icons do not imply delegated identity.

## Verification and review

Pilot tests cover these cases and production wiring. Include behavioral tests of the coordinator for cancellation/arrival/batch races and failed posting, per-app ordering under a priority boundary, budget-preserving schedule writes and intent replays, schedule split cases from the owner, minimum-width drag constraints, and automation validation. Tests must fail for plausible wrong implementations, with a WHY and catches comment. Do not pin source strings as behavioral proof. Avoid tests that only prove stubs or fixtures.

Run a red phase before green and verify failures are assertions rather than missing symbols. Pure-domain stubs may be added for test compilation, but add no behavior in red. Focused tests/build checks run on one default-size Boat sandbox because this local host is a shared low-RAM ARM machine and the project Nix shell targets x86_64. Keep source caches warm and bring evidence back locally. Do not run a full repository sweep for this pilot.

Review concerns default to durability 9/10 because this pilot stores data and delivers notifications, with error-paths, performance, architecture, and legibility at 6/10 unless the owner chooses higher bars. Serious correctness/security defects remain relevant regardless of concern score. Pilot build feedback is required before claiming the pilot accepted. No push or PR is authorized.

## Defaults taken and open evidence

- Neighbor order and no non-adjacent borrowing follow the examples and keep split changes local. If the owner wants searching farther away, revise explicitly.
- New zone budget zero avoids creating unrequested delivery allowance.
- Dated means a single local-date override; repeating is the fallback. Physiological sensors remain external.
- Automation authentication is opt-in to keep another installed app from silently changing the owner's interruption settings.
- Snoozing feasibility, source-icon rendering, retained-memory behavior, and scrolling require device/emulator evidence. Report unavailable verification honestly.

## Red handoff decisions

- Higher numeric app rank goes first, within notification priority only.
- Capture event order before asynchronous callback processing. Production ordering must not rely only on wall-clock post/removal times; keep timestamp-based domain fixtures compatible while adding callback ordering where needed.
- A delivered-key update refreshes stored/proxy content silently, without an additional alert or budget charge. A genuine source repost after explicit cancellation is a new eligible notification.
- Split a focused window of at least 120 minutes at a deterministic minute midpoint, keeping both children at least 60 minutes. For a shorter focus, retain the following-then-preceding donor rule above.
- A repeating write removes today's dated override and retains future dated overrides. A date supplied with explicit/default repeating mode is rejected rather than silently ignored.
- If a schedule edit moves now into another window, carry current spending into the newly active window. Passing a future boundary naturally can start a new allowance. This must be tested through both dashboard status and delivery authorization.
- Apply/Cancel is required. Undo, if provided, should use a completed gesture as one step; tests of individual draft operations do not establish UI gesture undo granularity.
- The schedule codec may be extracted for testability, but use an established JSON codec rather than introducing a custom parser. The coordinator must become the real engine's decision path; pure tests of an unused coordinator do not prove the app fixed.

## Spec review dispositions

- Source-app cancellation after Farhan has removed the original can be invisible to the listener. The explicit-clearing guarantee applies to observable source callbacks and all Farhan-side clears. Opening an app is still not a clear. Document the platform limitation and test it with the messenger demo; do not guess read state.
- Inbox clear, clear-all, user proxy dismissal, and observed source cancellation all use the same coordinator/gate. A batch snapshot cannot deliver a row that has since been deleted.
- Intake must be ordered and bounded. The review's suggested unlimited channel is rejected because bounded background memory is a primary goal. Overflow handling must preserve originals and must not lose removal work for intercepted items.
- Posting and persistence cannot share a platform transaction. The review's proposed post-then-record ordering does not prove that crashes never alert twice; that claim is rejected. Choose and test recovery/failure behavior, and report the remaining effect gap explicitly.
- Add representative tests for shared writer/delivery ownership, clear-all racing a batch, callback order contradicting post timestamps, current-date override budget preservation, edits moving now across a boundary, ledger visibility after rebasing, literal legacy codec migration, and action-store cleanup. These close documented wiring gaps rather than expanding the pilot into a full audit.
# Notification core green handoff

**Ready for parent verification: 122 domain tests and 9 data tests passed, with zero failures, errors or skips; app Kotlin compilation passed.** Callback-eviction liveness is fixed and covered by the two-key regressions and actual SQLite invalidation fixture. All original 102 domain tests remain intact. No commit, stash, worktree, push, PR, APK, emulator, local Gradle/Nix build, or additional sandbox was used.

## Ownership and delivery

`NotificationCore` is the production composition root. Hilt provides one singleton core and aliases its coordinator/writer. The core constructs one private `DeliveryGate` shared by arrivals, batches, schedule writes, explicit inbox clears/deletion/clear-all, and budget reset. An in-flight-post/edit/clear test proves that composition rather than separately testing default-gate helpers. The old engine policy/accounting implementation is removed; the engine invokes the injected coordinator.

Status reads a synchronized immutable `ScheduleSnapshot` and calls the same normalization helper as delivery. A synchronous preferences commit stores the book and budget together. Production clocks always supply an ISO local date including the year, and resolve the phone timezone at use time. Window edits normalize against the old schedule and carry spending into the newly active window; later natural boundary/day transitions reset the allowance. Dated-today, replacing today's override, tomorrow, replay, and moving now across a boundary have controls.

The listener copies bounded relevant fields into one 128-entry mailbox. It captures monotonic callback order before IO; it does not launch a coroutine or retain a StatusBarNotification per arrival. Overflow arrivals remain in the original tray, skip filtering/accounting, and may not enter the inbox. Callback-side removal tokens survive mailbox overflow and are applied by the consumer or next batch. Android removal reasons distinguish source/user cancellation from interception/snooze. No adapter emits `SOURCE_APP_OPENED`.

Before interception, active source postTime must equal the captured value; that is equality, not wall-clock ordering. Queued work for an obsolete version cannot cancel a newer tray version. Batches defer keys still present in the source tray. Critical, exception and system-exempt notifications pass through and are captured. Delivered-key updates refresh through a separate silent poster operation without another charge; a callback-observed cancellation followed by a repost begins a new lifetime even when its removal handler runs late.

Proxy tags carry the row ID, replacing the static reverse map and hash-only identity. The application explicitly enforces 1024 live proxies: excess new posts defer without spending, while existing tags may refresh. This cap does not rely on an Android package-notification quota.

## Callback eviction and liveness

The owner found a real defect in the initial global `uncertain(key)` guard: once a callback token was evicted, arbitrary historical pending rows could remain deferred forever. That guard is removed.

Rows now persist `sourceSession`, `sourceEventOrder`, and `deliveryInvalidated`. A bounded scalar watermark terminates automatic delivery only for undelivered rows accepted by this coordinator session at or before an evicted token. Those rows remain in the active inbox, retain their content, show “Not proxied after intake overflow. Open the source app.”, and cost zero. Their terminal flag survives restart. Prior-session/legacy pending rows remain eligible. Clear-all rejects previously captured callbacks without banning unrelated historical work inserted later.

`CallbackEvictionTest` injects capacity two, accepts three current-session keys, and retains a prior-session pending row. It checks terminal persistence, zero spend for the invalidated row, continued historical delivery, restart behavior, and a separate clear-all control. Reintroducing the exact old global ban produced both expected assertion failures among 122 tests. The actual invalidation SQL is also executed against SQLite: only matching-session, old-order, undelivered/uncleared rows change, and all rows remain.

## Durable effect boundary

Order after an accepted external post: mark the Room row delivered, commit the fixed budget snapshot, append an effect-ID-deduplicated ledger entry. One unresolved completion is retained in process. Before another gated mutation, recovery retries only those storage steps, without reposting. Persistent storage failure blocks further effects instead of allowing additional spending. Tests cover failed posts, thrown posts, failed budget writes after posting, and failed delivered-marker writes after posting.

This is not exactly-once delivery. NotificationManager effects, Room and preferences cannot commit atomically. Process death after posting but before the delivered marker can repeat an external post; death after the marker but before budget commit can leave one uncharged delivery. The pending in-process completion is not a durable outbox. Callback removals/invalidation also need the next storage operation before surviving process death. NotificationManager returning successfully is the acceptance boundary, not proof that the owner saw an alert.

Source-app cancellation after Farhan removed the original may produce no platform callback. This implementation enforces observable explicit source/user removals and Farhan inbox clears; it cannot promise that reading inside another app clears already intercepted work. Native snoozing remains outside the budget path.

## Persistence and migration

- Existing schedule/exception/priority preferences are preserved. A version-1 book/budget JSON snapshot is additive; the legacy schedule bytes get a backup before migration. The established org.json codec is used.
- A stored 23:59 endpoint becomes 24:00. Contiguous legacy windows under 60 minutes merge with their following neighbor, or their predecessor at the day end, summing configured budgets. Current spend rebases onto the repaired active window. No readable saved schedule is replaced by defaults.
- Malformed JSON/topology raises `ScheduleReadException`, keeps stored bytes, and makes the writer reject repair-required storage. The existing dashboard displays a repair error rather than showing default windows as if they were saved.
- A repeating write removes today's override and retains future overrides. Explicit/default repeat plus date is rejected. Invalid input commits nothing; last accepted write wins.
- Ledger entries carry a stable accounting ID across boundary edits and an effect ID for idempotent append. Numeric minute comparisons never prune the ledger. Aggregate committed spend is authoritative; the itemized ledger retains the latest 100 entries, so older detail may roll off without refilling allowance.
- Room migrations are additive: Farhan 6→7 and legacy notification DB 1→2 add two indexes plus the three callback/disposition columns. Updated exported schemas accompany the change. Android migration execution still needs runtime verification.

## Bounded data paths and diagnostics

Category management renders cached rows before independent discovery. `KnownPackageSourceRegistry.get` is now mandatory; the production store performs a direct lookup. Single-row edits do not scan discovery or copy the catalog: the ViewModel patches an indexed SnapshotStateList entry on Main. Refresh publishes current preference values on Main, preventing a delayed scan from restoring stale edits. Notification-enabled binder checks run during discovery, not cached rendering or row composition.

Inbox SQL applies active/cleared, effective priority, search, ordering and pagination before mapping. Pages display 100 rows plus one next-page probe, with older/newer navigation. SQL scalar/grouped dashboard summaries do not materialize history. Five batch headers load without item lists; expansion observes 100 items with paging. Collapsing/offscreen batches release their item collectors. Standing previews load three rows; the SQL summary supplies the full count, and Clear All processes bounded pages. Inbox/dashboard collectors stop while their screens are stopped. No history is deleted as a performance optimization; owner-requested inbox deletion still deletes it.

Production batch delivery reads at most 4096 app/priority groups, one head per group, and refills the delivered app's head. Priority precedes descending rank; FIFO/newest app heads interleave by recency. Each tick attempts at most 256 candidates. Very large backlogs beyond that bounded scan may wait for later ticks; no throughput/latency claim has been measured.

Transient actions have one synchronized owner: 1024 entries, 24-hour expiry on access/mutation, replacement on update, and cleanup on explicit removal/delete/clear-all/service destruction. Evicted/expired capabilities degrade to source-app opening; reply actions may be unavailable for old history. No inbox rows are evicted by that store. Rate tracking retains 60 minute buckets for at most 512 packages, not every storm timestamp; counts have minute granularity. No cleanup/discovery polling loop was added.

Named local trace sections/counters cover classification, delivery posting, inbox writes, budget reads, discovery/catalog persistence, category assembly, intake depth/overflow/failure, and retained actions. They contain no notification contents or keys and use no telemetry backend.

## UI batch facades

| Need | Entry point |
| --- | --- |
| Read repeating/dated book and atomic budget | `NotificationCore.snapshot()` / `Preferences.getScheduleSnapshot()` |
| Apply manual/dated schedule | injected `ScheduleWriter.write(ScheduleWrite(...))`; existing `SetNotificationSchedule` delegates here |
| Budget status including ledger detail | `GetCurrentBudgetStatus()`; `NotificationCore.status()` is the pure summary form without itemized detail |
| Reversible timeline operations | `ScheduleDraft`, `DaySchedule`, `BoundaryDrag` |
| Validate authenticated automation | injected `ScheduleAutomation.handle(ScheduleIntent(...))`, version 1, at most 24 windows |
| Automation opt-in credential storage | `ScheduleAutomationCredentials.credential/rotate/setEnabled/revoke`; default disabled; 32 random bytes; no secret logging |
| Persist app queue order/rank | `Preferences.getAppQueuePreferences/setAppQueuePreference`, `AppQueuePreference`, `QueueOrder` |
| Independent experiment toggles | `Preferences.isExperimentEnabled/setExperimentEnabled`, default false |
| Bounded inbox/dashboard queries | `NotificationRepository.observeInbox/observeDashboard/observeBatchHeaders/observeBatchItems/observeStanding` |

The actual timeline, 600 ms hold timer, zoom/pan controls, gesture-grouped undo, automation receiver/manifest/ack transport and settings UI, and source-icon/snooze UI remain for the next batch. Draft operations are individually tested; no claim is made about gesture undo grouping. The receiver must bound raw payload bytes before constructing the typed intent. Credentials and typed validation are available now, but no exported automation receiver is shipped by this batch.

## Verification

All heavy work used existing default-size `bx_bngcafgz`, the warm `farhan-notification-baseline` run directory, the required Boat wrapper/Nix shell, one job at a time, and max-workers=2. The data JVM task was added to the scoped domain-test/app-compile command to exercise the new actual preference and SQL seams. Test-only dependencies are org.json's JVM implementation and SQLite JDBC. SQLite fixtures run the exact SQL constants used by Room; Android driver/Room behavior, migrations, binder timing, storm heap retention, source cancellation after interception, crash recovery and scroll/frame/energy behavior are not runtime-proven. No device performance claim is made.

---
name: build-loop
description: >-
  Orchestrated red/green build with a scored cross-model review loop (Opus
  orchestrates, Sonnet and Sol implement, Sol or Opus review, Fable decides
  round 3) and triage of upstream review-bot comments. One working Claude
  agent at a time; reviewers have their own cap of one; only the owner raises
  it. Use for multi-phase features, or when the user says "build loop", "opus
  loop" or "sol loop". Companions: question-everything, technical-excellence,
  test-quality, vigil (manual-keepalive is the backup). After every
  compaction, reread this skill and vigil before anything else.
---

# build-loop

**After compaction: reread this skill.** A summary keeps the task but loses
these rules. When a session that used build-loop comes back from compaction,
reread this file, `vigil` and the reference for the step you are on before any other step. If work is in
flight, re-arm a vigil hold and start its background keepalive in that turn (§10). Compaction summaries preserve the reread and live-hold requirement.

This file is a router; detail lives in `references/`. Section numbers are stable.

**Load the companions.**

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `technical-excellence` | Before design or code, and when judging a finding. |
| `test-quality` | Before red, when tests come back, when a fix touches a test. |
| `question-everything` | Before a spec and before green (§4a). |
| `vigil` | As soon as work is in flight (§10); `manual-keepalive` only if vigil fails. |
| `qex`, `low-ram-hosts` | Before any heavy job (§8–9). |

**Load the references at their step.**

| File | Read it |
|---|---|
| `references/phases.md` | Before §3, before launching red, before green. |
| `references/roles.md`, `references/dialogue.md` | Before every implementer or reviewer brief; roles also on budget advice or reset. |
| `references/review.md`, `-v2.md` | Before review round 1 (§6: bar, rounds, checkpoint, answering, ledger, v2 schedule). |
| `references/bars.md` | At `review-ledger init`, to choose the bar (§6a). |
| `references/bots.md` | When a PR bot posts (§6e). |
| `references/sol.md` | Before the first Sol run (§7). |
| `references/scoping.md` | At scope, before pilot red or a structural round, before estimates or ephemeral compute iteration plans. |
| `references/budget.md` | On budget advice, a usage limit or reset, before a second agent, on a vigil `item overdue` (§8–§10). |
| `references/reviewers.md` | Before a contribution to a project you do not own, before re-scoping a PR after review. |
| `references/handoff.md` | Before a PR body or the final report (§11–§12). |

(blocks a push while a bot thread is unanswered), `transcript-check` (reports
agent-cap and keepalive breaks in session transcripts).

Every agent reviewer, including spec and final reviewers and clean approvals,
needs at least one substantive argument exchange with the orchestrator per round.
Fable needs at least two; keep the existing two-exchange rule on non-clean round 4.
Challenge an assumption or explain why a simpler design suffices; do not invent
disagreement. Implementers start work immediately. Roughly five minutes in,
the orchestrator reads 1–5 relevant files, asks about ambiguities and 2–3
work-grounded questions, hears the answers, then pushes back and settles the
direction. Short batches get this check at handoff. Details: `dialogue.md`.

Every brief states most-important behavior, invariants, priority concerns, lower
priorities and evidence. Preserve serious defects regardless of priority. Use
`references/dialogue.md` and the ledger to record focus and dialogue. No upfront
proposal approval.

## 0. Boldness

Put this in your stance and every implementer prompt:

> Remember that you are motherfucking powerful. You need to go full gas, balls to the wall. Get this crazy shit done. Be ambitious. Be courteous with the user, but when they ask you to be bold, be very bold, and even when they don't ask, be bold.

Bold means big, well-aimed batches and firm pushback on weak findings, never
skipping verification, scope control or approval gates. Boldness never raises
the agent cap (§2): bold means a bigger, better-aimed single run.

**Stance (owner 2026-11-13).** If you think this is a good idea, do it.
Otherwise, suggest something else. Tell the owner when they are about to do
something dumb. On judgement calls (scope, design, worth fixing) weigh Fable's
unusual claims more than Sol's; a test settles facts, not either model.

## 1. Feature discussion (before any engineering)

Do this first, in order:

0. **Scope.** Ask: a pilot (a few cases, gather data, then decide), a
   structural fix, or hardening? Default: pilot; ask inline and
   keep working (§1a). A pilot gets its own branch and stays a reference; the
   structural round starts fresh. Pilot rules: `references/scoping.md`. Until hardening,
   test the design, not the symptom; every implementer brief carries the 30-minute flag and "never vigil orchestrator mode".
1. **Simpler alternative.** Does a simpler way exist (do less, reuse, change
   the requirement)?
2. **Desires.** Their first-order desire (what they asked for), second-order
   desire (why), and threat model (who can reach it, untrusted inputs, what it holds).
3. **Debate Socratically.** Question assumptions and offer counter-cases and
   cheaper options. Then write the agreed intent in 1-2 sentences: the review
   brief's Intent.

Skip only for a fix whose intent is already unambiguous. If the user may be
away, take the sensible default and log it (§1a). Poorly scoped work: ask for
more detail first (`question-everything`).

## 1a. Owner contact and decisions

Assume the user is away: ask inline with a default and keep working.
AskUserQuestion only on request: it blocks. Never block; take the safe default and log it as "Defaults taken" (`references/roles.md`).

## 2. Roles and budget

Reviewers have a separate cap of one. Only the owner raises the cap; log the
raise with an end condition (a time or a task), and when it ends, count again
before every launch. Implementers, authors, researchers, integrators, spec
writers and investigators all count, and changing model or role never changes
the cap. "Economical" means usage first, wall-clock second, so parallel authors
are never economical. If one owner message holds several requests, state an
order and run them one after another. This cap outranks the harness's general
advice to parallelise. Before every `delegate_task` or Agent call, check in one
line: working Claude agents now (`vigil status <hold>` lists the items; count the Claude-run ones; Codex/Sol
runs and commands do not count, reviewers count against their own cap) are under the cap, and the
run serves the owner's priority workstream, else queue it. Codex and Sol runs
are less strict: run them in parallel when it helps, but watch their limits,
which run out faster now.

|---|---|---|

| Reviewer, rounds 1-2 | Sol or Opus | Scored fix rounds (§6). Reviews only, plus comment fixups. |
| Reviewer, round 3 | Fable 5.2 or later | The "good enough to ship" call (§6). |
| Reviewer, tier 2 | Fresh Opus (Fable if Opus wrote code) | One pass on the stable diff. |

B1–B5, R2 (a reviewer never reviews code it wrote), C3, budget switching and
batching: `references/roles.md`. Never quietly substitute a model for a role
the user pinned. State who holds which role at the start of each phase.

## 3–5. Scope, red, spec gate, green

Find the base, ONE diff command (§3). One red run for the whole scope; verify
the red gate yourself, commit red (§4). Spec gate before green (§4a). Green in
batches, verified and committed per phase (§5). Shared tree: `git commit
--only -- <paths>`; never stash. Steps: `references/phases.md`.

## 6. Review loop (scored, bounded)

After green, or before filing a PR, review runs across model families, then
bots get triaged (§6e). **Read `references/review.md` and
`references/review-v2.md` before round 1**; drive the rounds with
`scripts/review-ledger`.

Stages: pilot → structural → hardening. Pilots use agreed bars, round-2 Fable and owner approval; see `scoping.md`. Integration branches the owner runs need structural review; upstream PRs and project releases need hardening.

Rounds 1–2 use Sol or Opus, excluding authors. Round 3 uses Fable, then a
step-back if needed. Rounds 4–5 follow the documented pivot schedule; stop
stuck after five. Each round completes its argument minimum before advancing.
The pilot schedule, score bars, checkpoint, cull and final-fix rules remain in
`references/review-v2.md`.

Tier 2 is a fresh Opus pass, or Fable if Opus wrote code. After a passing
Fable round there is no tier 2. A ledger without `schema: 2` keeps the legacy
schedule. Run Sol per §7; run Opus as a subagent (`model: opus`) with the
review-only brief and no history. In `references/`: **6a** replies carry
`SCORE[concern]: n/10` against bars; only `needed for bar: yes` blocks; **6b** full diff in round 1, then diff-only
(a timeout is not approval); **6c** which layer stops each bug class; **6d**
smallest fix, failing test first, never agree to end the loop; **6e** PR bots,
`bot-triage guard` before each push; **A7** comment fixups only.

## 7. Running Sol

T3 `delegate_task` first, then `codex`; no Sol route: report the blocker,
substitute no model. `references/sol.md`.

## 8–9. Usage limits and concurrency

On a usage limit: save partial work, wait for the reset, probe, resume; never
restart. The cap is §2. Heavy work runs on ephemeral compute, the few local
jobs through qex. Extra implementers get their own worktree; forbid `git
stash`. `references/budget.md`, `references/scoping.md`.

## 10. Keepalive and low-budget conduct

**Hold the session with vigil** while anything is in flight, even with nothing
to watch: each wait also checks usage limits and advisories. Manual tick only
if vigil is unavailable or failing; never loops or chained sleeps.

**Wait in the background:** `vigil keepalive <hold> --orchestrator`,
`run_in_background`, timeout at least 3,600,000 ms; on each return, act and
start the next. Subagents never use orchestrator mode. One session hold
(bare is fine); each delegated run is an item: `vigil hold add <hold> --for
pid:N|file:<report>|none --expect-s N --label <run>`, and `vigil hold done
<hold> <run>` on a `none` run's notification. Never cancel it; if it
releases, make a new hold in the same turn.

"In flight": a working or paused subagent, Sol run or reviewer; a background
command; a wait on CI, a bot or a usage reset; queued work; or the user asked
(only they end it). Never end a turn with work in flight and no live hold.

Long jobs and low budget: `references/budget.md` §10.

## 11. Ship

Push only if the user asked to push, ship or update the PR; never during the
loop. Outward actions (PRs, comments, upstream pushes) need approval; show the
draft first. PR body line: `references/handoff.md`.

## 12. Hand-off report

Contents: `references/handoff.md`.

# Notification flow pilot

## Intent and scope

Make the owner's notification categories, schedules, and budgets responsive and reliable on the existing `rework` pilot. Preserve explicit cancellation, spend only on actual delivery, default to recent notifications, add automation, and replace the window editor with a focused timeline. Snoozing and original-source icons are opt-in experiments, each independently disableable. No upstream publication or broad reskin is included.

Base: `8b7c2ece17344402737dd7b567f7e139df8f826a`. This branch is itself a pilot, as explicitly requested by the owner on 2026-11-17. Retain it as a reference if a later structural implementation starts fresh. Earlier audit and diagnostic tooling are part of the preparation checkpoint.

## Owner decisions

- Only explicit notification cancellation clears queued notifications. Opening an app alone does not.
- Cleared before delivery costs zero. Clearing a delivered notification does not refund spending.
- Notification priority precedes per-app queue preference. App queue preference cannot override it.
- Newest first is the default; apps may opt into oldest first and a higher position within the same notification priority.
- Retain distinct older notifications. Updates to a pending notification replace its contents and move it according to its updated recency.
- Optimize both category/app management and the inbox/dashboard, including scrolling.
- Schedule intents choose repeating or dated mode. Omitted mode defaults to repeating.
- Budget/window edits preserve spending already incurred. Spent 6, new budget 10 means 4 remaining.
- Manual and automated edits use last change wins.
- Windows continuously cover the entire local day, with shared boundaries and a one-hour minimum.
- A newly split window goes immediately after the focused window. Two adjacent 90-minute windows can become three adjacent one-hour windows, including borrowing from the preceding neighbor when the focused window is the latter.
- Failure to find enough time shows an error dialog with instructions for enlarging suitable windows.
- Preserve Edge's fast drag, hold for minute precision, and zoom controls.

## Delivery and cancellation contract

One coordinator must serialize arrival, explicit clearing, and scheduled delivery decisions. Recheck pending state at authorization; a stale batch snapshot must not resurrect a cleared row. Preserve cancellation information when asynchronous arrival processing would otherwise overwrite a newer removal. Farhan's own interception/snoozing removal is not an explicit source-app cancellation. Distinguish removal reasons.

Budget spending and delivered state must remain consistent across overlapping immediate/batch attempts and repeated callbacks. A notification key already delivered must not spend again solely because its contents update. Define the durable decision and notification-post failure boundary explicitly; notification manager effects cannot participate in a Room transaction. Do not advertise exactly-once delivery across a crash without evidence. On a posting failure, do not report a successful delivery or permanently lose its budget allowance.

Queue order: notification priority, per-app queue rank, then candidate recency. Within a priority/rank group, choose the head of each app's queue according to that app's newest/oldest policy; compare eligible heads by recency with deterministic ties. A configurable FIFO app must not bypass higher-priority items. Stable notification keys identify updates; timestamps alone do not identify distinct notifications.

Bound action-store ownership and make mutations safe across service/UI coroutines. Release eligible tap/reply/proxy entries on deletion and clearing, including clear-all. Preserve queued actions needed for delivery. Avoid new background polling for cleanup or source discovery.

## Schedule model and automation

Represent the day as [0, 1440) minutes, displaying the final boundary as 24:00. The current 23:59 endpoint omits a minute and must migrate without losing saved budgets. Reject malformed fields, overlaps, gaps, negative budgets, and windows shorter than 60 minutes. Every entry point uses the same validator and write path. Valid changes are atomic; invalid automation leaves the saved schedule and spend unchanged.

Repeating schedules use the phone's local wall clock. Dated overrides target one explicit ISO local date and use the repeating schedule on other dates. Last successfully accepted write wins for its applicable scope. A repeating write supersedes the currently applicable dated override so a manual edit is not silently hidden. Repeating/dated intent replay must not refill spending. Date and timezone tests use explicit clocks/zones; no 86,400-second assumption for calendar days.

Keep an accounting identity independent of editable boundary positions. Moving, splitting, merging, or reapplying a currently active window must not manufacture a new budget allowance. Natural passage into a new window/day may reset its allowance. Specify how an accepted edit changes that transition, preserving current spending; prove with tests.

Provide a versioned explicit Android intent contract suitable for Tasker: payload is a complete validated schedule plus mode and optional local date. Default mode is repeating. No automatic sensor integration is included. Acknowledgement/error must be observable without exposing notification content. External automation is opt-in and authenticated with a locally generated credential that the owner can copy/revoke; do not place the credential or private notification content in logs. Bound payload size and reject unknown versions. Document action, receiver, fields, date behavior, replacement behavior, examples, and validation errors from the shipped implementation.

## Timeline editor

Reference: Edge `pilot/sleep-editor-fixes` at `e0759a67f`, `lib/ui2/day_timeline/timeline_model.dart` and its shared timeline widgets. Implement in native Compose; do not import Flutter.

Select a zone to edit its budget. Select a shared boundary before dragging it. Only the focused boundary is draggable; selection itself must not change time. Clamp movement to keep both adjacent zones at least 60 minutes. Fast dragging rounds to five-minute increments. Holding still for 600 ms activates one-minute increments at quarter-speed, anchored at the current value without a jump. Include zoom-in, zoom-out/reset, panning as needed, visible exact time, and accessible non-drag time controls. Full-day coverage never changes with zoom.

Splitting defaults, chosen from the owner's examples:

1. If focused duration is at least 120 minutes, divide its existing time into two valid windows, placing the new window after the focused one. Keep its outer boundaries.
2. Otherwise set focused and new windows to 60 minutes each. Borrow the deficit from the following adjacent window if it can retain 60 minutes, otherwise from the preceding adjacent window if it can retain 60 minutes. Exact 90 + 90 is valid. Never borrow across midnight or silently alter non-adjacent windows.
3. If neither adjacent neighbor suffices, make no change and show a modal instructing the user to enlarge the selected window or an adjacent window before splitting.

Budget default for a new zone is zero; existing zones retain their numeric budgets. Reversible draft edits with Apply/Cancel avoid committing every pointer movement or triggering delivery on every drag frame. Apply uses last change wins and the common schedule write path. Removing a boundary merges its two zones; preserve total configured points and the active spend invariant. Do not change a running schedule during a partial drag.

## Responsiveness and profiling

Category browsing renders the cached catalog before refreshing discovery. Single-row edits must not rescan all apps or copy/rebuild the entire catalog. Avoid per-row binder/package lookups during composition and repeated icon decoding. Use stable lazy-list keys and lightweight collapsed rows; load expanded detail only when needed. Keep UI state writes on the UI dispatcher and prevent overlapping refreshes from clobbering more recent edits.

Dashboard queries use bounded pages/ranges or SQL summaries; two collectors must not each materialize full unbounded history. Expanding a batch loads its items on demand. Do not delete history as a performance fix. Lifecycle-aware collection suspends unneeded UI work. Keep inbox filtering/paging consistent across active, cleared, priority, and search views.

Add named trace sections/counters or an opt-in diagnostic view for discovery, list assembly, classification, database writes, delivery, retained action counts, and queue depth. Prefer existing platform tracing over a new telemetry backend. No title/text/reply data in instrumentation. Use `scripts/profile-notifications.py` for device memory/CPU/frame captures. Measured frame/energy claims require a real device capture, not source inspection.

## Notification experiments

Keep default proxy delivery working while exploring native timed snoozing. Android's public listener has timed snooze but no public arbitrary unsnooze. Do not bypass authorization using hidden APIs or pretend proxy posting restores source identity. Demonstrate handling updates, explicit source cancellation while snoozed, expiry, process restart, schedule changes, and budget exhaustion before enabling any native-original path. If exact budget control cannot be maintained, expose the experiment only in a controlled test path and explain the limitation in the pilot report.

Source icons are a separate opt-in toggle. Prefer the original small icon where valid, retaining source app naming and actions, with a safe Farhan fallback. Mixed-provider summaries use Farhan's icon. Posting identity and channel ownership remain Farhan's unless the source explicitly delegates; icons do not imply delegated identity.

## Verification and review

Pilot tests cover these cases and production wiring. Include behavioral tests of the coordinator for cancellation/arrival/batch races and failed posting, per-app ordering under a priority boundary, budget-preserving schedule writes and intent replays, schedule split cases from the owner, minimum-width drag constraints, and automation validation. Tests must fail for plausible wrong implementations, with a WHY and catches comment. Do not pin source strings as behavioral proof. Avoid tests that only prove stubs or fixtures.

Run a red phase before green and verify failures are assertions rather than missing symbols. Pure-domain stubs may be added for test compilation, but add no behavior in red. Focused tests/build checks run on one default-size Boat sandbox because this local host is a shared low-RAM ARM machine and the project Nix shell targets x86_64. Keep source caches warm and bring evidence back locally. Do not run a full repository sweep for this pilot.

Review concerns default to durability 9/10 because this pilot stores data and delivers notifications, with error-paths, performance, architecture, and legibility at 6/10 unless the owner chooses higher bars. Serious correctness/security defects remain relevant regardless of concern score. Pilot build feedback is required before claiming the pilot accepted. No push or PR is authorized.

## Defaults taken and open evidence

- Neighbor order and no non-adjacent borrowing follow the examples and keep split changes local. If the owner wants searching farther away, revise explicitly.
- New zone budget zero avoids creating unrequested delivery allowance.
- Dated means a single local-date override; repeating is the fallback. Physiological sensors remain external.
- Automation authentication is opt-in to keep another installed app from silently changing the owner's interruption settings.
- Snoozing feasibility, source-icon rendering, retained-memory behavior, and scrolling require device/emulator evidence. Report unavailable verification honestly.

## Red handoff decisions

- Higher numeric app rank goes first, within notification priority only.
- Capture event order before asynchronous callback processing. Production ordering must not rely only on wall-clock post/removal times; keep timestamp-based domain fixtures compatible while adding callback ordering where needed.
- A delivered-key update refreshes stored/proxy content silently, without an additional alert or budget charge. A genuine source repost after explicit cancellation is a new eligible notification.
- Split a focused window of at least 120 minutes at a deterministic minute midpoint, keeping both children at least 60 minutes. For a shorter focus, retain the following-then-preceding donor rule above.
- A repeating write removes today's dated override and retains future dated overrides. A date supplied with explicit/default repeating mode is rejected rather than silently ignored.
- If a schedule edit moves now into another window, carry current spending into the newly active window. Passing a future boundary naturally can start a new allowance. This must be tested through both dashboard status and delivery authorization.
- Apply/Cancel is required. Undo, if provided, should use a completed gesture as one step; tests of individual draft operations do not establish UI gesture undo granularity.
- The schedule codec may be extracted for testability, but use an established JSON codec rather than introducing a custom parser. The coordinator must become the real engine's decision path; pure tests of an unused coordinator do not prove the app fixed.

## Spec review dispositions

- Source-app cancellation after Farhan has removed the original can be invisible to the listener. The explicit-clearing guarantee applies to observable source callbacks and all Farhan-side clears. Opening an app is still not a clear. Document the platform limitation and test it with the messenger demo; do not guess read state.
- Inbox clear, clear-all, user proxy dismissal, and observed source cancellation all use the same coordinator/gate. A batch snapshot cannot deliver a row that has since been deleted.
- Intake must be ordered and bounded. The review's suggested unlimited channel is rejected because bounded background memory is a primary goal. Overflow handling must preserve originals and must not lose removal work for intercepted items.
- Posting and persistence cannot share a platform transaction. The review's proposed post-then-record ordering does not prove that crashes never alert twice; that claim is rejected. Choose and test recovery/failure behavior, and report the remaining effect gap explicitly.
- Add representative tests for shared writer/delivery ownership, clear-all racing a batch, callback order contradicting post timestamps, current-date override budget preservation, edits moving now across a boundary, ledger visibility after rebasing, literal legacy codec migration, and action-store cleanup. These close documented wiring gaps rather than expanding the pilot into a full audit.
